what_it_does: Neutral-atom quantum computers trap individual atoms using laser light and use them as quantum bits (qubits); to perform a two-qubit logic operation, current designs physically move atoms close together, which introduces latency and errors. Quantum error correction (QEC) is a technique of spreading one logical qubit of information across many physical qubits so that errors can be detected and corrected without disturbing the stored value; the surface code is the most widely studied QEC layout. This paper proposes a way to do two-qubit gates between groups of atoms without moving them, by using two different atomic species whose quantum interactions have different strengths at different distances: the between-species interaction falls off slowly with distance (allowing long-range gates between groups), while the within-species interaction falls off quickly (keeping operations within a group local). Groups are interleaved on the chip so that a technique called lattice surgery — merging and splitting logical qubit patches — can connect them with high bandwidth. The design is validated through circuit simulations and algorithm benchmarks.
